chapter_theme: The second half of Perumpanatruppadai finishes the road to Kanchi, through the fisherfolk's settlement, the Brahmin village, the port of Neerpeyarru, the toddy-sellers' houses, the lighthouse, the grove farmers and the shrine of the god on the serpent bed, then praises Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan's city, victory and court, scripts the bard's praise, and lists the gifts the king gives the same day before closing on his peaceful hill.
structure_note: Thirteen units against the core's fourteen; every boundary was moved to a sentence end, mostly the guide's verbs of promise and command (பெறுகுவிர், கழிமின், ஆர்குவிர், குறுகி). The first unit opens mid-sentence: the sentence starts at line 263 in chapter 4.

pattupattu:4:271-282.reading: At the settlement of the net-fishers who guard the banks of a deep tank that never dwindles even in a long summer, moving with their children through its dark pool, the guide promises the bards a toddy made from unpounded rice mash cooled in wide-mouthed baskets, mixed with malt whose flowered crust looks like the grubs in a snake's anthill, left two turns of day and night, matured in strong-mouthed jars, strained hot and squeezed by hand, served with roasted fish, until they stagger.
pattupattu:4:271-282.nuance: The brew is given step by step (mash, cool, mix in malt, ferment, mature in jars, strain, squeeze), so the guide's knowledge of how the poorest folk of the road make their drink is itself part of the promise that the road will feed the bard. இருமறை கழிப்பி (279) I take as two turns of day and night; it could also mean two coverings of the jar.
pattupattu:4:271-282.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 271-286: ends at line 282, where பெறுகுவிர் closes the promise of toddy and fish. The sentence itself begins at line 263 in chapter 4 (the fishers' huts), a chapter boundary that cannot be moved, so the unit opens mid-sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of what the road gives the bards, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the flowered crust of the malt

pattupattu:4:283-296.reading: A fisher-bard skilled at catching ties his line to a long bamboo rod with a green hide bag of raw-meat bait, and the split-mouthed vaalai that has seized the bait on the bent iron hook shies from the trembling shadow of the cane by the water; in the old deep pond thick with red-petalled kuvalai and blue lilies, where the god's bright flower that has bloomed like fire is left unplucked and the whole is like the wide sky at its fullness after the rain, the guide tells the bards to wear the many opened flowers the pluckers have thrown down, on the great festival day, and pass on.
pattupattu:4:283-296.nuance: The lotus is called the god's bright flower (கடவுள் ஒண்பூ) and is not taken (அடைதல் ஓம்பி), while the bards are told to wear the flowers that others have dropped: even flowers on the road follow a rule of what may be taken. Lines 291 and 292 compare something to the wide sky 'without lack' after the rain has stopped; I read the pond at its fullest, but the tenor is not fixed by the words, and the angler's and the fish's parts in 283 to 288 may belong to one image of the pond rather than to an act of fishing.
pattupattu:4:283-296.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 271-286 and 287-300: begins with பச்சூன் (283), after பெறுகுவிர் ends the previous sentence at line 282, and ends at கழிமின் (296), the command to wear flowers and pass on.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's direction along the road, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the pond full of flowers

pattupattu:4:297-310.reading: In the good houses of those who keep the vows, with a low pandal where the fat calf is tied and floors smeared with fresh dung, which the house fowl and the dog do not approach, where the hook-beaked parrot is taught the secret recitation, if the bards stay in the village of the guardians of the Veda, the bangled wife of fragrant brow, chaste like the small star that shines in the north, will knowingly cook for them the rice named after a bird and serve it with the fragrant buttermilk and butter of the red cow, slices of young pomegranate fried with pepper and mixed with fragrant leaves, and pieces of tender mango from the tall tree in fine pickle.
pattupattu:4:297-310.nuance: The street is marked by what keeps away as much as by what is there: the fowl and the dog do not come near, and even the parrot repeats the recitation (மறைவிளி), so the Veda is heard from the birds. 'The rice named after a bird' (பறவைப் பெயர்ப்படு வத்தம்) is given only as a riddle; I take it as the swan-named rice. The cook is the wife herself, praised for chastity in the same breath as for knowing what to cook (வயினறிந்து அட்ட).
pattupattu:4:297-310.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 287-300 and 301-318: begins at செழுங்கன்று (297), after கழிமின் ends the previous sentence at line 296, and ends at பெறுகுவிர் (310), which closes the promise of the Brahmin house's meal.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the Brahmin village's hospitality, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the wife's chastity

pattupattu:4:311-335.reading: When girls bathing with their playmates at the drinking ford let fall a golden earring, the jewel-coloured kingfisher hunting prey strikes it for a fish, cannot carry it to the lonely frond of the bird-filled palmyra and rests on the sacrificial pillar set up by Brahmins of learning who paid their hard debt of sacrifice, showing slowly like the dawn star above the Yavanas' swan lamp; past the bounds of Neerpeyarru, by the watered gardens crowded with ships that bring milk-white horses and northern wealth, in sandy streets of high mansions filled with traders and guarded by servants, in rich houses where the plough-ox and the milch cow do not come but rams and swans wander, girls with curved jewels, their fine cloth swaying like dew creeping along the soft kondrai branch, move like peacocks dancing on a great hill, gold anklets ringing, and after the striped ball play golden kazhangu on the pearl sand of their sky-touching terraces.
pattupattu:4:311-335.nuance: The port is marked by what does not belong to the farm: the plough-ox and the milch cow keep away from its houses while rams and swans walk there, and ships bring horses from the north. One sentence carries the earring from a bathing girl through a kingfisher and a palmyra to a Brahmin sacrificial post beside a Yavana lamp, so the poem's single image joins the port's peoples: women at play, priests at sacrifice, foreign craftsmen.
pattupattu:4:311-335.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 311-318 and 319-335: the core cut at 318 falls inside the phrase தோன்றும் நீர்ப்பெயற்று (318, 319). This unit runs from the bathing girls (311) to line 335, where the description of the port's houses and the girls' game ends in the participle ஆடும், which qualifies பட்டினம் in line 336; the next unit begins there.

thinai_evidence.note: the road through the port of Neerpeyarru, part of the guide's description of the patron's land

comparisons.tenor: the golden earring on the sacrificial pillar
the fine cloth with green strands swaying on the girls' waists
the girls' gait

pattupattu:4:336-345.reading: Near the port, at the toddy-sellers' houses whose green flags sway over doorways many enter and whose swept courtyards are strewn with red flowers, the guide promises the bards strong toddy with chunks of fat from the short-legged boar that, once a dark piglet wallowing in the mud made by the little water the brewing women spilled washing their bowls, was kept many days in a pit, fed on rice flour and not let go to its hairy sow.
pattupattu:4:336-345.nuance: The boar's whole life is told in three lines, from piglet in the brewers' runoff to a pit where it is fed rice flour and kept from its sow (பாயம் போகாது), so the guests' meat is shown as raised for them. கள்ளடு (339) is a genuine அடு, to brew, not the comitative.
pattupattu:4:336-345.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 336-352: ends at line 345, where பெறுகுவிர் closes the promise of meat and toddy; the lighthouse that follows begins a new sentence at line 346.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the toddy-sellers' hospitality, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

pattupattu:4:346-362.reading: Passing the harbour where at night a bright torch hung on an unroofed tower, rising to fight the sky like a pillar propping it, its hard top reached by ladders, calls the ships sailing the rough sea, the bards come to the lone houses of the grove farmers, roofed with withering fronds of coconut whose trunk is like the flank of a hill-like elephant, with yellow courtyards and fragrant gardens; there they will eat the big jackfruit of clustered segments from the low branch, the sweet water of tender coconut, the curved white fruit of ripe banana bunches like the cheek-tusks of a dark she-elephant, palmyra nungu and other sweet things, and when tired of these, the full tubers of the chembu.
pattupattu:4:346-362.nuance: The torch calls the ships (ஓடுகலம் கரையும்), with the verb used for a crow that calls guests, so the port too has a way of inviting strangers. The elephant is the measure twice, for the coconut trunk and for the curve of the banana: the farmers' grove is described in the terms of the hill.
pattupattu:4:346-362.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 336-352 and 353-368: begins with the lighthouse at line 346, after பெறுகுவிர் ends the previous sentence at line 345, and ends at ஆர்குவிர் in line 362, which closes the promise of the farmers' fruit; the last word of line 362 (பகற்பெயன்) already begins the next sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the grove farmers' food, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the unroofed tower that carries the torch
the elephant
the coconut trunk
the curved white bananas

pattupattu:4:363-392.reading: Through the long way of many trees in never-failing rich villages where tall areca palms stand like streaks of daytime rain among coconuts whose three-sided nuts fall and break the pots cooking rice for hungry travellers, and past many lands of good towns whose sky-touching walls are clothed with unfading painted creepers, the bards come to where the one on the serpent bed lies like a bull elephant lying on a kaanthal slope; there, in groves no sunlight enters but the cuckoo does, where kuruku creepers wound on kaanji trees drop striped flowers like the round sweets that cake-makers shape with treacle and dip in milk onto the shaded sand at the water's edge, they may empty blue pots of toddy shaped like the areca's swelling spathe, sit in great joy, play by day with young women whose foreheads carry the shark-mouth ornament like the young crescent and whose eyes are drowsy with drink, rest at the great flowered ford of unfailing custom, like heaven itself, with those who wait for the hour, then praise the god of great strength, play a little on their black-horned instruments, and pass on.
pattupattu:4:363-392.nuance: The god's town is not named; the serpent bed and the bull elephant lying on the slope identify him, and the bards' worship is brief: praise him, play a little, go on. The groves' pleasures (toddy, play with women) and the shrine sit in one sentence, likened as a whole to heaven (துறக்கம் ஏய்க்கும், 388), a line the Pattinappalai repeats at its line 104. In line 378 போல் stands as போ before னிழல் by sandhi.
pattupattu:4:363-392.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 353-368, 369-378, 379-388 and 389-407: begins at line 363, after ஆர்குவிர் ends the previous sentence in line 362 (whose last word பகற்பெயன் opens this one), and ends at கழிமின் (392), the command to praise the god and pass on.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide sends the bards to praise the god on the road; praise of a god sits under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the tall areca trunks
the god lying on the serpent bed
the striped kuruku flowers
the blue toddy pots
the shark-mouth ornament on the forehead
the flowered ford and its groves

pattupattu:4:393-411.reading: Kanchi: groves where a big-bellied female monkey snatches the ghee-trodden rice ball of the long-trunked elephant while its keepers look away, posts where tuskers' rage is tamed, deep long streets cut by strong chariots, many families of great fame whose strength never knew defeat, gates never shut, crowded with those who give and take, gardens ringed with thorn, a city of tall brick mansions that rises beautiful like the pericarp of the many-petalled lotus that bore the four-faced one from the navel of the tall blue god; as the jackfruit is praised for its fruit among the rich-branched trees that bear without flowering where flocks of birds gather, so among the cities of this wide world, clothed in the smelling sea and crowned by the sky, this old town of ancient valour, worshipped by many, excels in festivals.
pattupattu:4:393-411.nuance: The lotus from Vishnu's navel is a picture of the city's plan: the walled town is the flower and its great houses rise in it like the pericarp (பொகுட்டு); the Paripadal fragment on Madurai uses the same lotus, with petals for streets and the pericarp for the palace. The jackfruit 'praised for its fruit' among trees that fruit without flowering (கோளி) gives the town a rank among cities rather than a picture.
pattupattu:4:393-411.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 389-407 and 408-417: begins at காழோர் (393), after கழிமின் ends the previous sentence at line 392, and ends with மூதூர் at the turn of lines 411 and 412, which closes the description of Kanchi before the comparison with the Five begins.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's city, part of the praise of the patron (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the tall-housed town within its walls
the old town among the cities of the world

pattupattu:4:412-435.reading: Like the Five whose banner-crowned tall chariot crossed the great war that never ended, when all the hundred fell fighting on a field where the bodies of white-tusked elephants dragged blood like the dancing clouds of a red evening sky crowned with the waxing crescent, he roared at the place where the hostile foes who came against him with countless armies were destroyed: he is the lord of Kachchi, open-handed, a refuge to those who come in want; because his grace and his wrath are both ready, the lands of those who fought him become ruined commons and the lands of those who love him bloom with gold, and kings who want his friendship and kings without allies who want his help, bowing in many ways like waterfalls running to the sea, crowd with unfailing wealth, like people waiting at the hard-to-cross Ganges ford for the boat that cleaves its white waves, watching for their hour in the courtyard of his rich city.
pattupattu:4:412-435.nuance: Lines 422 to 424 state the king's double face in one balanced pair, அளியும் தெறலும் எளிய: the same readiness that makes him a refuge makes him dangerous, and the poem shows the result in land, ruined commons for foes and gold-blooming country for friends. The Five (ஐவர்) and the hundred (ஈரைம் பதின்மர்) are the Bharata war, used as a measure of victory.
pattupattu:4:412-435.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 408-417, 418-433 and 434-451: begins at அவ்வாய் வளர்பிறை (412), after மூதூர் closes the description of the city, and ends at செழுநகர் முற்றத்து (435), where the kings who wait for his audience are placed; the core cut at 433 fell between the simile of the Ganges ford and its tenor in line 434.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's victory and liberality (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the blood-dragging bodies of the elephants
the king roaring at the field of his victory
the kings bowing to him in many ways
the kings waiting with their tribute for his hour

pattupattu:4:436-447.reading: In his great city where the red-legged cock-dove nesting in the eaves of the mansion starts from its sweet sleep, afraid of the hard ringing of the smithy where the dark-handed smith hammers the curved rings for the great-trunked elephants' tusks, he sits among his flawless kin like the sun spreading its disc over the middle of the eastern sea, granting to those who seek justice and to those who seek their needs whatever they ask, with a clear sight that discerns between them and a heart that never closes in the debt of giving: approach him.
pattupattu:4:436-447.nuance: முறைவேண்டுநர் and குறைவேண்டுநர் (443) are those who come for a judgment and those who come for a need; the king answers both, and the clear sight that discerns between them (இடைத்தெரிந்து உணரும் இருள்தீர் காட்சி) is what makes the giving just. The frightened dove in the eaves lets the smithy's war-work be heard inside the king's house.
pattupattu:4:436-447.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 434-451: begins at பெருங்கை யானை (436), after செழுநகர் முற்றத்து (435) ends the sentence of the waiting kings, and ends at குறுகி (447), where the bards are told to approach him; the tiger simile that follows opens the bard's address.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's justice and giving (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the king granting to all who ask

pattupattu:4:448-461.reading: Like the striped tiger cub that longs to seize the spotted-faced elephant its mother has struck, you pay the debt owed to poets and break your enemies' guarded walls to take their crowns; your strong sword-hand will not agree to any work but victory; descendant of the Tondaiyar who live on plunder, warrior of warriors, hero of heroes, lord of the wealthy, foremost in battle: as spirits snap their fingers before the goddess of the thunangai dance, the big-bellied mother of the red one with green jewels who killed fierce Sur in the white-waved sea, so praising your great name of unceasing giving I have come, lord; may you live long: so the guide tells the bard to say.
pattupattu:4:448-461.nuance: The guide gives the bard the very words of his praise (மள்ளர் மள்ள, மறவர் மறவ, செல்வர் செல்வ) and the formula of arrival (வந்தேன் பெரும வாழிய நெடிது). கொண்டி உண்டித் தொண்டையோர் (454) says the Tondaiyar live on plunder, so what the king gives the bard is drawn from what he takes in war. Lines 457 to 459 are hard: I read அணங்கு நொடித்தாங்கு as spirits snapping their fingers before Murugan's mother, the goddess of the thunangai, but who snaps and for whom is not fixed by the words, and the tiger simile may belong to the line before.
pattupattu:4:448-461.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 434-451 and 452-475: begins at பொறிவரி (448), the tiger simile that opens the bard's address, and ends at நெடிதென (461), where the scripted praise closes.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's valour and giving, scripted for the bard (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the king's eagerness to take his enemies' forts and crowns
the bard praising the king's name

pattupattu:4:462-479.reading: When you have played the roomy great yaazh in due order and praised him with joined hands as custom knows, before you have finished telling your state he weighs the condition of this unlasting world and, wishing his own state to shine without end in the cool land of the naaval tree, strips from your waist the rag like moss and dresses you and your great family together in cloth bright as vapour, and with a glad face, looking on you again and again as on his children, stands and feeds you himself without tiring, spreading white bowls like flowering stars with rich pieces of many meats cooked by a skilled cook whose strong hand is scarred by the curved knife, long boiled grains of choice rice of the great red paddy, and sweet dishes guarded like nectar.
pattupattu:4:462-479.nuance: The king acts before the bard has finished asking (நின்னிலை தெரியா அளவை), and the poem gives his reason as a reckoning: he weighs the unlasting world (நில்லா உலகத்து நிலைமை தூக்கி) and wants the state of undying fame. He feeds the bard himself, standing (தான் நின்று ஊட்டி), looking at him as at his own children (மகமுறை); the order of the gift (rags off, new cloth on, food) is the order of other gift poems.
pattupattu:4:462-479.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 452-475 and 476-500: begins at இடனுடைப் பேரியாழ் (462), after the scripted praise ends at line 461, and ends at ஊட்டி (479), where the feeding closes and the gifts of ornament begin.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's giving to the bard, the gift the guide promises (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the bard's rags
the bright fine cloth
the white bowls spread for the meal

pattupattu:4:480-500.reading: He crowns your thick hair with a golden lotus like the moon in the misty sky, round which no bee hums, and has the viraliyar wear golden garlands that shine in their dark hair like lightning darting through the daytime rain of a season sky that has drunk from the rough sea; not content with giving a striped chariot yoked with four mated horses whose white manes look like the conches of the great sea, praised by the horse books, he adds the sky-going steeds and green trappings he took from the foes he routed in war, and sends you off that very day with his gift: he is the lord of the hill of shining falls, where kinnaras hum on haunted slopes, peacocks dance in the thickets, flowers shaken down by leaping stags lie in the glades, the female monkey sweeps the yards where the beasts sleep, and the sages who tend the red fire sacrifice with firewood that white-tusked elephants bring.
pattupattu:4:480-500.nuance: The poem ends naming the patron only as lord of the hill (மலைகிழவோனே), and the hill is described by its peace: beasts sleep in yards a monkey sweeps, and elephants carry firewood for the sages' fire, so the last picture of the war-king's land is of wild things serving a sacrifice. அன்றே விடுக்கும் (493) makes speed part of the gift. Line 481's அழல்தவிர் (our reading) against அழலவிர் (bright as flame) changes only the epithet of the golden lotus.
pattupattu:4:480-500.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 476-500: begins at மங்குல் வானத்து (480), after the feeding ends at ஊட்டி in line 479; the poem ends at line 500.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's gifts and his hill, the close of the guide poem (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the golden lotus
the gold garlands in the viraliyar's dark hair
the white-maned horses

links.note: The guide promises the bards rice toddy brewed by fisherfolk and roasted fish until they stagger; the couplet says do not drink, or let only those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy drink.
links.teaches: The idyll counts drinking to the point of staggering among the best hospitality of the road, given freely by the poorest folk, while the couplet makes drink the mark of one who forfeits esteem, so the ethics book is rejecting a pleasure the oldest praise poetry offered as part of the gift.

links.note: Both praise a wife as chaste like the northern star: here the Brahmin wife who cooks for the bards, in Purananuru 122 Kari's wife, the one thing he keeps while all else goes to Brahmins and bards.
links.teaches: In both poems the star-chaste wife stands at the centre of a house that gives to Brahmins and bards, but in the chief's poem she is what is kept back from giving and in the idyll she is the one who gives, so the simile marked the giving household from either side.

links.note: In the idyll a kingfisher strikes a bathing girl's golden earring for a fish and carries it off to a sacrificial pillar; in the Naladiyar quatrain a kingfisher takes the beloved's eyes for carp but does not dive, seeing her brow as a drawn bow.
links.teaches: The kingfisher's mistake about a woman's ornament or feature was a set conceit: the idyll lets the bird act on its mistake as part of a port scene, while the later love quatrain stops the bird short, turning the same error into praise of the woman's brow.

links.note: The toddy-sellers keep a boar in a pit for many days, fed on rice flour and kept from its sow, to serve its fat to the bards; the couplet says that if no one killed to eat, no one would bring flesh for sale.
links.teaches: The idyll describes exactly the chain the couplet condemns, an animal fattened in confinement to be served and sold, and offers it as a reward of the road, so the Kural's argument against buying meat cuts against a hospitality the guide poems praise.

links.note: The Paripadal hymn makes the god lying in waking sleep on the many-hooded serpent in the milk sea one of his three cosmic forms; the idyll places the one on the serpent bed at a grove shrine on the road where bards stop to praise him and play a little.
links.teaches: Together they show the serpent-bed form both as cosmic theology and as the god of a particular shrine on the road to Kanchi, so in the Sangam period the same image was already tied to local worship that a passing bard could visit.

links.note: The Paripadal fragment likens Madurai to the lotus from Mayon's navel, its streets the petals and the lord's palace the pericarp; the idyll has Kanchi's tall-housed town rise like the pericarp of the lotus from the blue god's navel that bore the four-faced one.
links.teaches: The navel-lotus with the central great house as its pericarp was a shared figure of city praise used for Kanchi as well as Madurai, so it was a convention for a Tamil capital rather than a legend of one city.

links.note: Purananuru 2 praises a Chera for feeding the armies without limit while the hundred fought the Five until they fell; the idyll uses the same war to say its king roared at his victory like the Five when all the hundred fell.
links.teaches: The pair shows two ways Sangam praise borrowed the Bharata war: the Chera poem keeps its king outside the war as the feeder of both sides, while the Tondai idyll puts its king in the victors' place, so the epic could measure a king's giving or his conquest.

links.note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
links.teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

links.note: Purananuru 185, by Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan himself, says the realm is a cart that runs well only if its driver is skilled and otherwise sinks in the mire of enmity; the idyll shows the same king's court running smoothly, justice and gifts granted to all.
links.teaches: Read beside the patron's own conditional maxim, the bard's portrait answers the king's worry with a finished picture: what Ilanthiraiyan states as a risk depending on the driver, the guide poem states as already achieved, which shows the work praise did for a king who wrote about failure.

links.note: The guide scripts the bard's praise of the patron (warrior of warriors, lord of the wealthy, of unceasing giving) as the way to his gifts; Arunagirinathar confesses that praising people as lotus-handed and clouds in giving, to beg from them, wounded his heart, and asks to serve Murugan instead.
links.teaches: The patron praise that the guide poem teaches as a craft with a sure reward is in the later hymn the very habit the poet repents, so the bard's profession that founded Tamil praise poetry became for the devotional poet the model of misplaced service.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai has a flesh-eating demoness dance the thunangai after the god kills Sur; here the bard's praise is likened to the finger-snapping before the goddess of the thunangai, mother of the one who killed Sur in the sea.
links.teaches: Both guide poems use the Sur victory and its thunangai dance, but the god's guide poem uses it to praise the god while the king's guide poem makes it the model for praising a man, so the form of Murugan's praise was lent to the praise of a patron.

links.note: Weighing the condition of the unlasting world, the king gives before the bard has finished asking; the couplet says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts.
links.teaches: The idyll turns the couplet's 'at once' into a patron's habit with its motive stated, wealth that will not stay given for fame that will, so the maxim had a heroic model in the bard's patron before it became a rule of the ethics book.

links.note: Both strip the suppliant's rag like old pond moss, dress him in new cloth and feed him meat and rice; Purananuru 390 ends by saying that kings with elephants do not even know such feeding.
links.teaches: The rag, cloth and meal follow a fixed order of the gift rite in both, and holding them together shows the idyll claiming for a crowned king the very hospitality that Purananuru 390 boasts only the lesser chief gives, so the boast was rhetoric and not a rule of rank.

links.note: Purananuru 361's patron gives golden lotuses to bards and garlands to the singing women and needs no one to tell him the world does not last; the idyll's king crowns the bard with a golden lotus and garlands the viraliyar after weighing the unlasting world (line 466).
links.teaches: Placed together, the golden lotus for the bard and the garland for the singing woman appear as a fixed pair of gifts tied to one stated motive, the patron's knowledge that the world does not last, which lets the Purananuru king face Death and makes the idyll's king hurry the gift.

source_issues: Line 481: our text reads அழல்தவிர் தாமரை; the tamilvu text reads அழலவிர் (bright as flame). Either is an epithet of the golden lotus; the reading is kept and the karu form is copied from our text.

The comitative -ஒடு lost its vowel sign after ய/ள in lines 293, 299, 320, 345, 434 and 492 (repaired in the core as flagged by show); karu forms such as குவளையொடு, கோழியொடு and புரவியொடு are copied as repaired.
Line 467 lost its first letter in the 2021 e-text (repaired from the 2000 version as யந்நிலை).
Line 308 prints யளை இப் with a space inside அளைஇ; it reads as one word.
Line 388 (பெறற்கருந் தொல்சீர்த் துறக்க மேய்க்கும்) is the same line as Pattinappalai line 104; it is a shared formula, not a copying error.
Line 271 begins in the middle of a sentence that starts at line 263 in chapter 4; the unit could not be moved across the chapter boundary.
